notes.1: (a) The majority of candidates made a good start to the paper and answered this question well. The most popular answers were that the government wanted to reduce unemployment, to increase economic growth and to increase competition. However, many answers did not go beyond generic answers, with no application to the case, and therefore did not move into the higher mark range for this question. Answers could have included application such as Peter had lost his job and was unemployed, Peter had an objective to expand his business so jobs will be created, vans are converted into motorhomes and the government supported new businesses by provided grants and free training. (b) The majority of candidates showed a clear understanding of penetration and cost-plus pricing methods. However, price skimming was sometimes confused with competitive pricing. Better candidates identified the pricing method and then went on to explain the advantages and disadvantages of each method, such as penetration pricing would set a much lower price than competitors in order to attract consumers to try the new product but this would result in lower, or no, profit per product. Weaker responses did not include how the pricing methods should be used but instead gave vague answers such as ‘this would be a good method to attract consumers’ without any indication of how the method would be effective. Application was often omitted and where it was included it was usually for identifying the product as motorhomes or the conversion of vans and large cars. The recommendation could have justified any of the three pricing methods but often weak justification for the rejection of the alternative pricing methods meant the response did not gain the highest marks.
notes.2: (a) The majority of candidates answered this question well. They identified that the business failed due to poor management of finance of the business. Application was often present as candidates included that the previous employer lacked management experience and was unable to pay its suppliers of car parts. Some candidates gave other likely reasons for the failure of the business such as over-expansion and failure to plan to adapt to change in the market. Application was often gained in this question but candidates did not always fully explain why the reason resulted in the failure of the business and therefore their marks were lower than they might have been. Weaker answers just ended with ‘and so this meant the business failed’. This is not an explanation of the reason. Better candidates did develop their answer and fully explained the reason in context to gain full marks. (b) Generally a well answered question. Candidates used the information provided in Appendix 2 and identified that the recruitment agency will cost a lot more to use than the job vacancy website. Candidates usually stated that asking family and friends was the cheapest of the three ways and they would be likely to suggest someone who would be trustworthy but not a wide range of candidates would be available and they would be unlikely to have the skills required. Weaker candidates thought the job vacancy website was set up by Peter and that people would routinely tell lies about their skills. Better responses stated that a wider range of people than family and friends would be likely to see the advertisement, but that it may not be seen by people with suitable skills amongst the many job advertisements on the website. The recruitment agency was the best explained of the three ways and the majority of candidates identified that it was the most expensive, included figures from Appendix 2 and included that they assured WA that they could provide suitable candidates for the three job vacancies. The recommendation often selected the recruitment agency as the most suitable given that the employees needed to possess many skills to undertake job production.
notes.3: (a) Again well answered by the majority of candidates although lack of application was the main reason for candidates not achieving full marks. The most popular answers were increasing customer loyalty, identifying customer wants so they could be satisfied and so that satisfied customers would spread the word to others leading to an increase in sales. There was often at least some application from the inclusion of the van conversions into motorhomes and identifying that job production was being used. 0450 Business Studies June 2019 (b) This question proved more difficult for weaker candidates. Vague answers such as ‘the business needs to consider sample size to ensure it gets accurate results’ were often given which did not answer the question. There were many answers that remained at Level 1 due to a lack of explanation as to why sample size, location and questions asked could cause questionnaire data to be inaccurate. Weaker responses stated that the sample was how long the questionnaire was or an actual sample of the product. The recommendation sometimes did not choose which of the three was most important and therefore did not answer the question. The most popular factor was the questions themselves as better candidates concluded that, even if the sample size was small or the location did not cover the target market, if the questions were clear and well-constructed then useful data would be gathered. Although there were also rewardable recommendations that argued that sample size or location was the most important in gathering accurate data.
notes.4: (a) Generally a well answered question. The majority of candidates identified an advantage such as the vehicle will meet the exact needs of the customers and therefore increase their satisfaction with the business. Popular disadvantages included, being time consuming, a more expensive production method or labour needing to be more skilled and therefore needed to be paid a higher wage. A minority of candidates incorrectly thought this was where jobs were specialised such as those in flow production and that the jobs were boring. Making reference to vehicles, vans and cars in answers was credited with application. However, only more able candidates included more than simple application. (b) Better candidates could calculate the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed and then draw conclusions based on the figures calculated. A minority of candidates tried to calculate liquidity, which was not possible from the figures in Appendix 3. Weaker responses just made comparisons of the figures between the two years, such as revenue increased by $5000, but could not go beyond this to calculate profit or profitability, hence these answers remained in Level 1. Recommendations did not often go beyond stating that profitability had fallen and Peter should be worried.
